title: Causes, effects and careful claims
cando: discuss causes and effects in health, the environment or society without overstating

about.text: In this lesson, you talk about why things happen and what they lead to, without claiming more than you know. You listen to two council workers discussing a local problem, read an article about a reservoir that is running dry, and write a balanced paragraph. Then you discuss a problem in your own area and agree on the likeliest cause.
goals: Suggest a cause carefully: It could be that…, may, might, partly.
Say what usually or probably happens: tends to, is likely to.
Follow a chain of effects: lead to, result in, which in turn.
Read an article about the environment and write a balanced paragraph.
Agree with a group on the likeliest cause of a local problem, and one action.

chapters.title: A problem near us
chapters.text:
In this lesson, we talk about causes and effects: why something happens, and what it leads to.
We start in a council office. Lena and Omar work for the council. Complaints about a local park have doubled, and they want to know why.
Listen to how carefully they speak. Omar says: It could be that this is the root cause.
He does not say: This caused it. He isn't sure yet, so he doesn't claim it.
Listen for three phrases. It could be that. This is likely to. And which in turn.
Which in turn joins a chain of effects. Litter attracts rats, which in turn puts people off using the park.
You also learn words for causes. A factor is one cause among several. The root cause is the deepest one, the cause behind the others.

chapters.title: Careful claims, clear chains
chapters.text:
The grammar has two parts.
The first is hedging. Hedging means showing how sure you are.
May, might and could mean: it's possible. The new flats may be a factor.
Tends to means: this usually happens. Litter tends to attract rats.
Is likely to means: this will probably happen. The problem is likely to get worse.
The second part is cause and effect. Lead to and result in join a cause to its effect. The cuts led to fewer collections. Fewer collections resulted in more litter.
Which in turn adds the next step in the chain.
One small point: after may and might, the verb never takes an s. Say: It may cause problems. Not: It may causes problems.

chapters.title: A reservoir running dry
chapters.text:
Next, you read a news article about a reservoir that is running dry.
Many people want one simple answer. The article gives three: the weather, the amount of water we use, and leaking pipes.
Notice how it deals with climate change. Long, dry summers are likely to become more common. But no single summer can be blamed on climate change alone.
That is a balanced view. It gives each cause its place, and it doesn't claim more than the facts show.
The article also builds a chain with words for the environment. A new plant would need a lot of energy. Unless that energy is renewable, emissions go up, which in turn adds to climate change.
Then you write a balanced paragraph of your own, about an environmental problem you know. Give more than one cause, say how sure you are, and finish carefully.

chapters.title: What's behind it?
chapters.text:
In the task, you discuss a local problem in a group. It could be late buses, noise at night, or rents going up.
Each person may have a different idea about the cause. That's normal, and it's useful.
Ask for evidence, and be fair to other ideas. You can say: That's probably part of it, but… Or: To some extent, yes.
Here is an example. One person says: I think one factor might be the roadworks. Another answers: That's probably part of it, but the buses are late on Sundays too. That is evidence, and it helps the group decide.
Then agree on two things: the likeliest cause, and one action you can take or ask for.
One clear action is better than five vague ones.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer text about causes and effects in health, the environment or society.
As you read, keep asking one question: does the writer prove this, or only suggest it?
Look for the careful words: may, might, likely, partly. A writer who uses them is often more honest, not less.
Then talk or write about it. Which claims did you believe, and why?

warmup.prompt: Your local park has more litter than last year. What do you think is the main reason?
choices: the bins are emptied less often
people care less than they did
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Most local problems have more than one cause, and in this lesson you learn to talk about them carefully.

conversation.title: Complaints about the park
conversation.setting: Lena and Omar work in the neighbourhood team at Northbridge Council. Complaints about Riverside Park have doubled since the spring, and they are trying to work out why.
lines: Lena
So, complaints about Riverside Park have doubled since April. Most of them are about litter.
Omar
I'm not surprised. The budget cuts have led to fewer collections: the bins are emptied once a week now, not three times. It could be that this is the root cause.
Lena
It's certainly a factor, but I don't think it's the whole story. The new flats on Mill Lane opened in March, so the park is much busier.
Omar
True. It gets really overcrowded at weekends now. And on the whole, more people means more rubbish.
Lena
Some residents also mention anti-social behaviour: groups drinking late and leaving bottles on the grass.
Omar
That might contribute to the problem, but we should be careful. We've had three reports about it, not thirty.
Lena
Fair enough. What worries me is what comes next. Litter attracts rats, which in turn puts people off using the park.
Omar
And an empty park tends to attract more trouble in the evenings. It's a vicious circle.
Lena
Exactly. And with the long summer evenings coming, this is likely to get worse before it gets better.
Omar
So what can we actually do? We can't tackle everything at once.
Lena
I'd start with the bins. It's the one thing we control, and it's likely to have the biggest impact.
Omar
Agreed. If we go back to three collections a week and the complaints fall, we'll know. If they don't, the cause may be partly something else.
Lena
Good. Let's take the figures to the manager on Monday.

questions.q: What are most of the complaints about?
questions.why: Lena says: Most of them are about litter.

questions.q: Why does Omar want to be careful about anti-social behaviour?
questions.a: There have only been three reports.
wrong: The police are already dealing with it.
questions.why: Omar says: We've had three reports about it, not thirty.

questions.q: What do they decide to try first?
wrong: closing the park in the evenings
writing to the people in the new flats
questions.why: Lena wants to start with the bins, because it's the one thing they control, and Omar agrees.

phrases.use: Suggesting a possible cause when you are not sure.

phrases.text: It's certainly a factor, but I don't think it's the whole story.
phrases.use: Agreeing that something is one cause, but not the only one.
Warning that there isn't enough evidence yet.
Showing how one effect leads to the next.

phrases.text: This is likely to get worse.
We can't tackle everything at once.
phrases.use: Saying you need to choose where to start.

phrases.text: It's the one thing we control.
phrases.use: Giving a practical reason for your choice.

items.meaning: One of several things that cause a situation or affect a result.
items.example: Cost was a big factor in our decision.

items.meaning: The main, deepest reason for a problem, often hidden behind the more obvious ones.
items.example: Late trains are annoying, but the root cause is the old signals.

items.meaning: A strong effect that something has on a person, a place or a situation.
items.example: The new road has had a huge impact on the village.

items.meaning: To be one of the causes of something. You contribute to something.
items.example: Stress can contribute to poor sleep.

items.meaning: To make something start suddenly, often something bad.
items.example: Cold air can trigger an asthma attack.

items.meaning: To become worse, or to make something worse.
items.example: The traffic has worsened since the bridge closed.

items.meaning: To start dealing with a difficult problem in a serious way.
items.example: The council has promised to tackle the housing shortage.

items.meaning: To do or use less of something.
items.example: I'm trying to cut down on sugar.

items.meaning: How clean or polluted the air in a place is.
items.example: Air quality is poor near the motorway.

items.meaning: Paper, cans, bottles and other rubbish that people leave on the ground in a public place.
items.example: The beach was covered in litter after the festival.

items.meaning: Behaviour that upsets or harms other people, such as shouting, fighting or damaging things in public.
items.example: Residents have complained about anti-social behaviour outside the station.

items.meaning: With too many people in it.
items.example: The trains are overcrowded in the rush hour.

items.meaning: Not completely; only in some ways.
items.example: The delay was partly my fault.

items.meaning: Partly, but not completely.
items.example: To some extent, I agree with you.

items.meaning: In general, when you think about everything.
items.example: On the whole, the new system works well.

sound.title: Joining words: which in turn
sound.explain: In natural speech, when one word ends in a consonant sound and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the two words join. Which in turn sounds like whi-chin turn. Cut down on sounds like cut dow-non. Worse in sounds like wor-sin. Listen, then say each group, joining the words.
groups: which in turn · which is · which affects us
cut down on · worse in summer · a lot of it
lines: Litter attracts rats, which in turn puts people off.
We need to cut down on car journeys.
The traffic gets worse in the evenings.

sayIt.instructions: Say Lena's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Do you sound careful and calm, not certain about everything?
lines: It's certainly a factor, but I don't think it's the whole story. The new flats on Mill Lane opened in March, so the park is much busier.
Fair enough. What worries me is what comes next. Litter attracts rats, which in turn puts people off using the park.
Exactly. And with the long summer evenings coming, this is likely to get worse before it gets better.
I'd start with the bins. It's the one thing we control, and it's likely to have the biggest impact.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Nobody says: This caused that. Each speaker shows how sure they are, or how one thing leads to another.
examples: It could be that this is the root cause.
That might contribute to the problem.
An empty park tends to attract more trouble in the evenings.
This is likely to get worse before it gets better.
Litter attracts rats, which in turn puts people off using the park.
spot.question: Which words show that the speaker is not sure? Which describe what usually happens, or what will probably happen? Which phrase joins a chain of effects?
spot.answer: ‘It could be that’ and ‘might’ show a possible cause, not a certain one. ‘Tends to’ describes what usually happens. ‘Is likely to’ describes what will probably happen. ‘Which in turn’ joins a chain: the litter brings rats, and the rats keep people away.

rules.title: Hedging: may, might, tends to, is likely to
rule: may, might or could + verb: a possible cause. The new flats may be a factor.
It could be that + a sentence: It could be that the bins are the root cause.
tend to + verb: what usually happens. Litter tends to attract rats.
be likely to + verb: what will probably happen. It is likely to get worse.
Soften a claim even more with partly, to some extent or on the whole.
rules.mistake: Not: This may causes problems. Say: This may cause problems.

rules.title: Cause and effect: lead to, result in, which in turn
rule: cause + lead to + effect: The cuts led to fewer collections.
cause + result in + effect: Fewer collections resulted in more litter.
After lead to and result in, use a noun or -ing: It led to people staying away.
which in turn adds the next step: Litter attracts rats, which in turn puts people off.
Can't show how A causes B? Say it contributes to B, not that it causes B.
rules.mistake: Not: The cuts resulted to more litter. Say: The cuts resulted in more litter.

practice.q: Litter ___ to attract rats and foxes.
practice.why: Litter is singular, so tends to: what usually happens.

practice.q: The problem is likely ___ worse in the summer.
The new flats may ___ a factor.
practice.why: After may, use the verb with no s and no -ing: may be.

practice.q: Fewer bin collections have ___ to more litter.
practice.why: lead to + an effect: have led to more litter.

practice.q: The budget cuts resulted ___ fewer collections.
Litter attracts rats, which in ___ puts people off.
practice.why: which in turn: the effect becomes the next cause.

practice.q: It ___ be that the new takeaway is part of the problem.
practice.why: It could be that … suggests a possible cause.

practice.q: Which sentence is the most careful?
options: Traffic is always the reason for asthma.
practice.why: may shows a possible effect, not a certain one.

practice.q: Cheaper rents may lead to more people ___ into the area.
practice.why: lead to + a noun or -ing: lead to more people moving.

practice.q: Smoking is one factor that ___ to heart disease.
practice.why: contribute to: be one of several causes.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a problem where you live or work: traffic, noise, litter, rents, or long waiting times at a clinic. Write four or five careful sentences about its causes and effects. Use may or might, tends to or is likely to, and lead to, result in or which in turn.
yourTurn.model: Traffic on our road has got much worse this year. One factor may be the new supermarket, which opened in May. It could be that the roadworks on the bypass are partly to blame too. Heavy traffic tends to push drivers onto side streets, which in turn makes those streets less safe. The problem is likely to continue until the roadworks finish in the spring.

text.title: Brenmoor Reservoir: where has the water gone?
text.body:
PRACTICE ARTICLE: Brenmoor and its reservoir are not real.

For the third summer in a row, the water in Brenmoor Reservoir has fallen to its lowest level for forty years. Sailing boats are sitting on dry mud, and a ban on watering gardens with a hose is likely to start next month. So what is behind it? The answer, it seems, is not one thing but several.

The first factor is the weather. The region has had three dry summers, and this year's drought is the worst since records began. Many people blame climate change, and scientists agree that long, dry summers are likely to become more common. However, they are careful to add that no single summer can be blamed on climate change alone.

The second factor is us. Water consumption in the area has risen by about 15% in ten years, partly because 4,000 new homes have been built. On hot days, people also tend to use far more water in their gardens.

The third factor is less visible. Brenmoor Water admits that almost a quarter of its water is lost through leaking pipes before it reaches a tap. Critics say that fixing the leaks would save more water than any ban.

The low water is already having an impact on wildlife. The reservoir's edges are an important habitat for birds, and two rare species of dragonfly have not been seen there this year. Local experts warn that the damage may take years to reverse.

What can be done? The company has proposed a plant on the coast that would turn sea water into drinking water. The problem is that it would need a great deal of energy. If that energy did not come from renewable sources, the plant's emissions would increase the region's carbon footprint, which in turn adds to the climate change that makes droughts more likely.

Most experts take a balanced view. The most sustainable answer, they say, is to treat water as the limited resource it is: fix the leaks, help people use less, and plan new homes with water in mind. As one local farmer put it: ‘Nobody is entirely to blame here, and nobody is entirely innocent. We all use the tap.’

gist.q: What is the main point of the article?
gist.a: The water is low for several connected reasons.
wrong: Climate change alone has caused the problem.
The new homes are the only cause.
gist.why: The article says the answer is not one thing but several.

gist.q: How does the article deal with climate change?
gist.a: as a likely factor, but not the only cause
wrong: as the main and only cause
as something with no link to the problem
gist.why: Dry summers are likely to become more common, but no single summer can be blamed on climate change alone.

detail.q: Why has water consumption in the area risen?
detail.a: partly because 4,000 new homes have been built
wrong: because farmers are using more water
detail.why: The article says consumption has risen partly because 4,000 new homes have been built.

detail.q: How much of Brenmoor Water's water is lost through leaks?
detail.why: The company admits that almost a quarter of its water is lost through leaking pipes.

detail.q: What has happened to the wildlife?
detail.a: Two rare species of dragonfly have not been seen this year.
wrong: The birds have moved to the coast.
detail.why: The article says two rare species of dragonfly have not been seen there this year.

detail.q: What is the problem with the plant on the coast?
detail.a: It would need a great deal of energy.
wrong: It would be too far from the reservoir.
detail.why: The article says the plant would need a great deal of energy, which could increase emissions.

items.meaning: Fair to all sides: it looks at more than one opinion or cause.
items.example: The article gives a balanced view of the problem.

items.meaning: Changes in the world's weather over many years, especially rising temperatures.
items.example: Climate change is likely to make heatwaves more common.

items.meaning: Gases, such as carbon dioxide, that cars, factories and power stations send into the air.
items.example: The company has cut its emissions by a fifth.

items.meaning: The amount of carbon dioxide that a person, a company or an activity adds to the air.
items.example: Flying less is one way to reduce your carbon footprint.

items.meaning: Renewable energy comes from sources that do not run out, such as the sun, the wind and water.
items.example: Our office now runs on renewable energy.

items.meaning: Able to continue for a long time without harming the environment or using up what we need.
items.example: We need a more sustainable way to heat our homes.

items.meaning: The amount of something, such as water or energy, that people use.
items.example: Energy consumption rises sharply in winter.

items.meaning: Something useful that a country, a company or a person has and can use, such as water, oil, money or skills.
items.example: Clean water is a precious resource.

items.meaning: The natural home of a plant or an animal.
items.example: Building on the wetland would destroy an important habitat.

items.meaning: A group of animals or plants of the same type. The plural is also species.
items.example: Several species of bird nest by the river.

items.meaning: A long period with little or no rain, when there is not enough water.
items.example: The drought has hit farmers hard this year.

model.title: A balanced paragraph
model.body:
Why is our river flooding more often?
Flooding in our town has become more frequent in the last ten years, and there is probably no single reason for it. Climate change is likely to be one factor, since very heavy rain tends to be more common than it was. However, it would be wrong to blame the weather alone. Hundreds of new homes have been built on fields that used to soak up the rain, which in turn sends more water into the river. Some residents also blame the council for not clearing the drains, and this may be partly true. On the whole, the evidence points to a mix of causes, so a sustainable solution is likely to need several changes rather than one.

write.task: Write a balanced paragraph of 100 to 150 words about an environmental problem you know: in your town, your country or your workplace. It could be flooding, air quality, litter, or the water or energy we use. Give at least two possible causes, say how sure you are, and end with a careful conclusion.
write.starter: There is probably no single reason for …
checklist: I gave at least two possible causes, and I did not blame just one.
I used may, might, tends to or is likely to where I was not sure.
I used lead to, result in or which in turn at least once.
My last sentence sums up without claiming more than I can show.

card.title: What's behind it?
card.situation: Your group lives or works in the same area. Choose one local problem: buses that are always late, litter, noise at night, a clinic with long waiting times, or rents going up. Each of you has a different idea about the cause.
card.goal: Discuss the possible causes carefully. Agree on the likeliest one, and choose one action you can take or ask for.

phrases: I think one factor might be …
It could be that …, but I'm not sure.
That's probably part of it, but …
On the whole, the likeliest cause is …
If we can only do one thing, let's …
prepare.notes: Choose a problem. Write two or three possible causes, with one piece of evidence for each. Then decide which cause you think is the likeliest, and one action you could take or ask for.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, you work in a group of three or four. Your teacher gives each of you a different cause to argue for. Discuss them carefully, agree on the likeliest cause, and tell the class your one action.
doIt.wehel: Let's discuss a problem in my area: the buses are always late. You are my neighbour, and you think the roadworks are the main cause. I'm not sure. Discuss it with me, and ask me for evidence. Then help me agree on the likeliest cause and one action. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: The 42 bus
lines: Kwame
So, the 42 bus. It's been late almost every morning since September. What's behind it, do you think?
Mei
I think one factor might be the roadworks on Bridge Street. The traffic there is terrible.
You
That's probably part of it, but I'm not sure it's the whole story. The buses are late on Sundays too, when the roads are quiet.
Kwame
Good point. It could be that they're short of drivers. I read that several routes have been cut.
Mei
Maybe. And since the new flats opened, the buses are overcrowded, which in turn means longer stops.
You
So we've got three possible causes. Which one is the likeliest?
Kwame
On the whole, I'd say the drivers. The roadworks only explain the weekday mornings.
Mei
To some extent, yes. But we don't actually know how many drivers they've lost.
You
Then let's not guess. Why don't we write to the bus company and ask for the figures?
Kwame
Agreed. And we should mention the Sunday delays. That's the best evidence we have.
Mei
Fine. I'll draft the email tonight and send it to you both.
compare: Did you give more than one possible cause?
Did you hedge the claims you could not prove: might, it could be that, to some extent?
Did you use evidence, like the Sunday delays, to decide which cause was the likeliest?
Did your group agree on one clear action?

canDo: I can suggest possible causes without claiming more than I know.
I can use may, might, tends to and is likely to.
I can explain a chain of effects with lead to, result in and which in turn.
I can read an article about the environment and write a balanced paragraph.
I can agree with a group on the likeliest cause of a local problem, and one action.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. What problem does the text describe? Who or what do you think is to blame?
reading.talk: Did the writer ever claim more than they could show? Find one cause that was only possible, not proven. Write three or four sentences about it, or discuss it with Wehel.

quiz.q: Cold air can ___ an asthma attack.
quiz.why: trigger: to make something start suddenly.

quiz.q: Litter is a serious problem, and the council needs to ___ it.
quiz.why: You tackle a problem when you start dealing with it seriously.

quiz.q: Heavy traffic ___ to poor air quality in the town centre.
quiz.why: contribute to: be one of several causes.

quiz.q: Prices are ___ to rise again next year.
quiz.why: be likely to + verb: what will probably happen.

quiz.q: Which sentence is the most careful?
options: The new road caused the floods.
The new road may have contributed to the floods.
The new road definitely made the floods worse.
quiz.a: The new road may have contributed to the floods.
quiz.why: may have contributed describes a possible cause, not a proven one.

quiz.q: When the river dries up, the birds lose their ___ .
quiz.why: A habitat is the natural home of a plant or an animal.

quiz.q: The amount of carbon dioxide that you add to the air is called your carbon ___ .
quiz.why: Your carbon footprint is the carbon dioxide you add to the air.

quiz.q: If I ___ about the job earlier, I would have applied.
quiz.why: Third conditional: if + had + past participle, then would have.

quiz.q: The minister is expected ___ resign next week.
quiz.why: Reporting with the passive: be expected + to + verb.

quiz.q: This time next year, we ___ in the new office.
quiz.why: This time next year + will be + -ing: something already going on then.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the council conversation in pairs, then replace the park with a real problem from the learners' own area. Every claim must be hedged: It could be that…, partly, to some extent.

Day 2: the task. Groups of three or four discuss one local problem, each learner arguing for a different cause. Each group agrees on the likeliest cause and one action, and presents both in one minute.
Day 3: talk about the book: which claims were proven, and which were only possible? Then two learners read their balanced paragraphs aloud, and the class listens for the hedges.
